en: Record of Observations on the Commentary to the Bodhisattva Precepts Compiled by Dan-gui (Jinshi) and his attendant Gu-xin (Gao) (Note:
"丹霞" *Danxia* refers to the lineage or school; "今釋澹歸" *Jinshi Danguī* is the author Dan-gui;
"造侍者古心" *Zaoshi Zhe Guxin* indicates the attendant who assisted in the compilation, Guxin.)
In the *Jingxian Yanyi*,

the Tiantai school of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) establishes four vehicles— Zang, Tong, Bie, and Yuan— and does not posit a separate "Sudden" (Dun) teaching, as it subsumes the Sudden within the Perfect. Although...
However, the sudden within the gradual is subsumed by the Perfect [Teaching] of Tiantai, whereas the sudden within the sudden is not subsumed by the Perfect Teaching of Tiantai.
Please clarify this by means of that very teaching itself. It enumerates five grades for the external ordinary person (*bāiwǎn*). First is the mind of initial sympathetic joy (*suíxǐ xīn*):

either encountering a virtuous friend (*shànzhīshí*) or through a scripture, one hears the wondrous principle in its perfection, gives rise to perfect faith and understanding, and cultivates perfect practice, thereby achieving...
The ten modes of contemplation (*daśa-dhyāna-yāna*) culminate in the ultimate *vajra* final mind. When these ten contemplations form a vehicle, they constitute the fruit of perfect consummation;
like a box meeting its lid, how could this not be sudden? Nevertheless, one enters the stage of perfection through the profound and clear elucidation of each of the ten contemplation chapters.

The purification of the six sense organs is called "semblance-understanding. Upon reaching the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), at the first abode, the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*), one begins to realize a portion of the three virtues (*tridharmakāya*).
In each successive stage, one destroys a portion of ignorance (*avidyā*); when the forty-one portions of ignorance are exhausted, one finally achieves Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).

Is this not gradualness within the sudden? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "In principle, there is sudden awakening; by means of awakening, [all obstacles] are simultaneously eliminated. As for phenomena..."
Because causes are gradually eliminated in successive order, there is the principle of simultaneous dissolution; thus, there is no need for gradual shattering or gradual realization.
This is why gradual shattering and gradual realization occur: they pertain to the "semblance-understanding" (*sādṛśya-adhimukti*) of the Perfect Teaching.

The ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitute semblance-understanding, while the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) constitute true middle-way wisdom. Understanding is semblance, while realization is truth. Realization is attained through understanding; [the two] are unified.

It cannot be called "gradual within the sudden. When it pertains to the fruit of gradualness within the sudden after realization, it is the sudden cause within gradualness at the time of understanding;
therefore, it is called "sudden within the gradual. This constitutes the Perfect (Yuan) inclusion of Tiantai.

Now, there are those of the most superior faculties who, upon their initial sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), immediately reach the ultimate *vajra*-final-moment mind. Flowing against the current, they immediately enter the [Bodhisattva] stages.
It is immediate movement, immediate stillness; it is the holy and the ordinary; it is the internal and the external.

It is neither horizontal nor vertical, neither single nor double, neither central nor peripheral, neither head nor tail. At the moment of realization, there is nothing realized; how could there be anything to be destroyed?
Since there is nothing to be destroyed, there is also no one who realizes. How, then, could there be any doctrine of gradual destruction or gradual realization? Thus...
It is the "sudden within the sudden," and therefore it is not subsumed under the Perfect [Teaching] of Tiantai.

Now, although the Sudden and the Perfect originally possess no dual principle, once they are distinguished in terms of understanding (*jñāna*) and realization (*adhigama*), they appear as two separate matters. If one attains realization through understanding, there is gradual practice;

if one gives rise to practice from realization, there is fundamentally no sudden understanding. This is what this school claims to be its own unique "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings. Tiantai understood [this].
It does not establish itself within these; it is not that the Perfect [Teaching] subsumes the Sudden, for this is the "Sudden within the Sudden," which is not encompassed by the Perfect.
Since the Teaching has the sense of being gradual, this [Sudden within the Sudden] is likewise not included within the Teaching.
Furthermore, those who discuss the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) necessarily take the *Avataṃsaka* as their primary authority. The Master of the Commentary (*Suzhu*) cites it, stating:

"Upon the very first stage of the Abiding of the Initial Resolve (*Prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), one attains perfect enlightenment; all its merits cannot be fully extolled by the Buddhas of the three periods of time. And yet, it further says: "The initial resolve..."
The mind abides. One realizes one portion of the three virtues and breaks through one portion of ignorance; thus, there remain forty portions of ignorance that have not yet been broken.
A single perfect mirror is established, and within this expedient means, it is divided into forty-one portions.

The three virtues are used as a metaphor for light, and ignorance as a metaphor for defilement. Whether breaking through first and realizing later, or realizing first and breaking through later, it does not go beyond this one portion. Thus...

If one manifests only one part of the light while leaving forty parts of defilement intact, it becomes a mirror entirely composed of impurity; even when reaching the ground, being half-light and half-defilement, how could it be perfectly luminous?

If you claim that the essence of luminosity is inherently perfect and that the characteristics of defilement merely gradually depart, then what is called "luminosity" is merely intellectual understanding, not realization.
It is also but a partial realization, not a perfect realization. As the Elder Fangshan said: "The Ten Abodes..."

The initial stage—namely the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*)—are mutually interpenetrating.
Within a single stage, fifty dharma-gates are attained; within each stage, two thousand five hundred gates appear simultaneously in both their general and specific aspects.

One establishes a single perfect mirror: when there is one, one appears; when there are many, many appear; when it is partial, it appears partially; when it is complete, it appears completely. Thus they intermingle in layers upon layers.
Upon entering, it manifests layer upon layer; people perceive it as being partially or fully manifest, yet these layered reflections appear with a sense of sequence.
The fundamental mirror is perfectly luminous, possessing neither sequence nor non-sequence. Thus one sees the eight-year-old dragon girl attaining Buddhahood in a single thought-moment.
How could there still be the ignorance of fragmentation in the Immaculate World (Vimalā-loka) to the south?

If this stage of the first abode were not a perfect realization, then the meaning of "immediately attaining perfect enlightenment" would also be inconsistent, as would the statement that with the very first mind of sympathetic joy, one perfectly hears the wondrous principle:
that one dharma is all dharmas, all dharmas are one dharma, and they are neither one nor all.
To give rise to perfect faith and understanding while cultivating perfect practice—wherein one single practice constitutes all practices—is for both meanings to fail to be established.
Furthermore, according to the principle that "sudden awakening causes the vehicle to be merged and eliminated upon awakening," even the principle itself no longer exists;

how then could phenomena still present obstacles? If there were phenomena yet to be removed, there would necessarily remain a principle not yet eliminated. This meaning is clear: these two cannot coexist. Therefore...
Fangshan said: "There are three kinds of five stages and ten grounds: first, practicing with provisional designations, provisional wisdom, and provisional suchness;
second, practicing with partial truth, partial realization, and a portion of true suchness; third, practicing and realizing instantaneously the perfect suchness of the Buddha-realm."

As in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, only the stages of abandoning delusions across the ten grounds are established. In the *Renwang jing*, there are five stages and ten grounds, wherein one gradually practices from the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and accumulates merit over many lifetimes.
Some claim that the abandonment of delusions occurs prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*), while the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) occurs upon the grounds;

this is said to be the provisional teaching’s gate of conventional *tathatā*. According to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, bodhisattvas at the stage of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) see their nature only partially, continuing thus up to the tenth ground.

It is not yet fully clear. This refers to the partial cultivation and partial realization of *tathatā* (Suchness). According to the *Yingluo jing*, when a Bodhisattva enters the stage of the sages, they simply abide within the flow of the *dharmatā*;
with each thought-moment extinguished, they naturally flow into the great ocean of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

This constitutes the orthodox teaching of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Yet, Fangshan still says that the intent of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not so; for when consciousness ceases, the objects of the senses perish.
It is suddenly cut off. Even if an ordinary person were to remain in the world for a hundred years or even for many kalpas, they would not see within themselves even a moment’s transition;
they would not see that they will become a Buddha, nor that they have already become a Buddha, nor that they are currently becoming a Buddha.

What further birth could there be where one does not become a Buddha? What further birth could there be where one becomes a Buddha? As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* says: "Except for those who have attained sudden enlightenment."

Furthermore, this Dharma is not something that conforms to ordinary understanding; were it not for an extraordinary gate of awakening, one would certainly not believe in such a boundless state of a Great Man.
This is the realm of non-action.

The Commentary states: Regarding the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*), it consists in non-arising; if it arises, it is unconditioned (*asamskrta*) and of a nature that is "fictive form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Why is this? The essence of the precepts is simply the nature itself. "Unconditioned" means non-arising. When all natures do not arise, some may suspect that they are arising.
Arising is itself nature; nature is itself non-action (*anabhisamskāra*). Non-action cannot be seen; it is seen by means of provisional form (*rūpa*). How could form possess action?
If action were to produce form for the sake of seeing, how could action possess action? How could seeing possess seeing? The sūtras and śāstras are mutually quiescent;

this is merely because they are obstructed by the notion of "having non-action. To have non-action is simply to be without non-action. Those who speak of non-existence cite the *Ratnavyūha* (The Jewel Garland).
The Sūtra states: "The precepts of all noble ones and ordinary beings take the mind as their essence. Some say that the True Dharma (paramārtha-satya) is the essence of the precepts;
others say that the vow (praṇidhāna) is the essence of the precepts. There is no separate "unmanifest" (avijñapti).

Since the mind is unmanifest, and the True Dharma and the vow are likewise unmanifest, once the unmanifest has already been established, there is no separate unmanifest. As the Great Sūtra says: "The noble practice observes and analyzes impermanence. The Ācārya..."

World-Honored King, when one contemplates and analyzes the objective realm, it is only the manifestation of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). One does not speak of non-manifestation (*avijñapti*), nor of the non-manifestation of form, nor the non-manifestation of mind.
Since the discussion of non-manifestation has already been concluded, one does not speak of non-manifestation here; all [terms] contain the negating particle "not" (*na*) regarding non-manifestation.

As for those who speak of existence, they mean that the power of the mind is great, capable of producing all phenomena and drawing forth retribution. There is a distinct goodness that arises based on a teacher, or...

Is it that based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or based on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), there is the arising of non-informative action (*avijñapti*)? Is this [non-informative action] existent?

Is it that which can produce all phenomena, up to and including their karmic fruition (*vipāka*), and is it existent? Is it that which arises based on what has been taught by a teacher, or based on meditative concentration and the path, and is it existent?

Is non-informative action existent? Yet you yourself say: "The Lesser Vehicle also speaks of non-instruction (*avijñapti*). Thus, the discussion of the non-existence of non-informative action is concluded. Great!
Riding upon the clear precepts is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). As the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "Sin and non-sin are unobtainable.
Regarding the perfection of *śīla*, it says: "If sin and non-sin are unobtainable, can *śīla* be obtained? Can its essential nature (*svabhāva*) also be obtained?
To illustrate this, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* provides an analogy: "Just as when there is a face and a mirror, a reflection appears. It is like this.

Because there is action (*kriyā*), there is non-action (*akriyā*); yet the causal conditions cannot be apprehended. Just as the image, the mirror, and the face are all unapprehendable, how could non-action possibly be apprehended?
Having already explained that there is no such thing as non-action, those who maintain that non-action exists do so merely through conventional expressions indicating its absence.
What we now refer to as "action" or "non-action" is used only by virtue of the precepts (*śīla*).

There is that which can maintain, and that which is maintained; there is attainment and non-attainment; there is that which can be guarded and maintained, and there are skillful means by which [the precepts] may be brought to fulfillment.

One should know that there exists separately the "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*); it is able to maintain the mind of ethical discipline, and thus they may be distinguished. As for the unmanifest, it is the general essence of all phenomena;
within the dharma of ethical discipline, it is specifically termed the "precept-essence" (*śīla-svabhāva*). The unmanifest subsumes the precepts, whereas the precepts do not subsume the unmanifest.
Non-action (*avijñapti*) cannot encompass the precepts while desiring non-action to exist; yet non-action can encompass the precepts while desiring non-action not to exist.
This is "small non-action," which creates an obstruction for the single mind (*ekacitta*). The reason the single mind is unobstructed is because of non-action.
The reason non-action is unobstructed is because non-action is non-existent. Because non-action is non-existent...
All things exist. There is the Buddha’s non-action and the absence of the Buddha; there is the sentient being’s non-action and the absence of the sentient being;

there is the living being’s non-action and the absence of the living being; there is the insentient’s non-action and the absence of the insentient. All things have no agent because all things are non-existent.
The Buddha cannot be apprehended; sentient beings cannot be apprehended; both the animate and the inanimate cannot be apprehended. That which cannot be apprehended is itself also unapprehendable.

There is no non-action, yet it is precisely through non-action that there is action. When one speaks of negation, one does not further affirm; when one speaks of affirmation, one does not further negate.
It is merely speech, it is merely speech. Why engage in dispute?
The unconditioned precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) takes non-action as its essence. Both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*) likewise take non-action as their essence.

The unconditioned precept shared with concentration and the Path is the general [category] of this non-action. The precept shared with concentration and the Path is the specific [category] of this non-action. Concentration is shared with...

Within the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arises. Within the vision of the truths (*darśanamārga*), which is conjoined with the Path, non-informative action arises;

this refers merely to the arising of the precepts. How could non-informative action have arising or non-arising? Master Zhiguan says that it also arises during the contemplation of the mind through the Middle Way. Other masters say: [it does not].

Upon entering meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one is able to generate non-informative action (*avijñapti*). It is not generated within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). Some say that it is generated prior to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) even within the realm of desire;
others say it is generated by a superior mind (*adhimātra-citta*) and not by an inferior mind (*hīna-citta*), nor by a neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*).

This refers to the non-generation of the precept itself; even if it were generated, it would be a distinct non-informative action. As for the actual generation of non-informative action, there is not a single person nor a single moment in which it occurs [without the aforementioned conditions].
There is not a single place where it does not arise. Even when discussing its arising and ceasing, it is simply the arising and ceasing of the precepts.

Within this arising and ceasing, there is difficulty and ease, as well as duration and brevity; these are likewise the difficulty, ease, duration, and brevity within the non-manifestation (*avijñapti*) of the precepts.
In the correct teaching, non-action (anabhisamskāra) is such that there is not a single person, not a single moment, and not a single place where it does not arise.
Non-action encompasses both movement and non-movement; it encompasses both stillness and activity; it encompasses both the great and the small; and it encompasses both good and evil.
All phenomena—whether moving or non-moving, still or active, great or small, and good or evil—all possess the essence of non-action, and yet they are non-action.

It is neither moving nor non-moving; neither ceasing nor proceeding; neither large nor small; neither good nor evil. It is not that there is a separate entity, for all things possess the essence of non-action (*avijñapti*).
Because they all possess this essence of non-action, it is called "having non-action. Because there is no separate entity, it is called "not having non-action.
This is merely a matter of whether the essence of the non-action of precepts exists or does not exist. How could non-action itself have existence or non-existence?
There are no three obstacles, for the nature [of reality] is fundamentally nameless. It acquires its substance through speech; when it functions, it is but like a dream or an illusion.

To speak of "obstacles" means that they are hidden when temporarily separated. This hiding is not a lack of separation, and this separation is not a lack of hiding. It is, for example, like failing to see a bright pearl.
It is not that there is no one who sees; nor is it that the jewel is absent simply because it is momentarily unseen. The Commentary (Shu) directly judges this, saying:

"The absence of the three obstacles is merely a discourse on the nature [of reality]. Since afflictions (*kleśa*) are ever-present, they are not termed 'obstacles'; however, karma is fundamental and grave.

Even when emerging from the gravity of afflictions, one eventually reaches the obstacle of retribution (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*), which is likewise rooted in the gravity of afflictions. Thus, afflictions are truly the basis of karma."

The Master [states that] because he does not speak of obstructing afflictions (*kleśa*), they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Since all natures are without intrinsic nature, afflictions are without intrinsic nature.

Depending on the continuity of mindfulness, the duration of time—whether long or short—is determined. When a gust of wind blows away a fragment of cloud, it is not called an obstruction; when heavy clouds veil the sky, it is called a karmic obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*);
when accumulated clouds persist for ten days or more, it is called a retributive obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*). If the original heavens do not subside, the obstructions likewise remain as they were.

There is none. Having repented the seven heinous offenses and the ten grave transgressions, they no longer constitute an obstruction. Once the retributions of hell and the hungry ghosts are exhausted, they likewise no longer constitute an obstruction.

Yet, even so, it is not that they are not obstructions; rather, it is in the sense that they are not obstructions. If one realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*), then one knows that the fundamental sky has no nature of being a fundamental sky, and that the manifest clear sky has no nature of being a clear sky.
It is the same with heavy clouds and accumulated gloom: they have no inherent nature because they are not created. They do not exist.

Therefore, it is said: "Examine this closely. Then both the Buddha and sentient beings are merely designations (*adhivacana*). Of what use is the precept? Because the nature (*dhātu*) was not yet known, the precepts were established.
Once the nature is known, even the precept lacks inherent nature. Within this absence of nature, that which is called "conducive" refers to the meaning of the precept;
that which is called "obstructive" refers to the meaning of the nature. To be without obstruction is itself the nature.
Meaning: The meaning of precepts is the absence of intrinsic nature; the meaning of obstacles is the absence of obstacles. To speak does not obstruct existence or non-existence;
yet how could there be an obstacle to that which is neither spoken nor attained?
The Preface to the Sutra:
The Radiance of the Divided Light. The Buddha Vairocana emits light; this light informs the Buddhas upon the thousand petals. The Venerable Nāgārjuna appears upon his seat.
The mark of the full moon: one hears only the sound of the Dharma, yet does not see its form. Thus, the Buddhas and Patriarchs are held together as one.

Within the light there is the complete teaching; within the teaching there is the complete light. Within the eyes there is complete hearing; within the ears there is complete seeing. The environment and the inhabitants are equally hidden;
these two are one. The three bodies are equally revealed; they are neither one nor three. This inconceivable light exists only upon the thousand petals of the lotus.
The Buddhas are the light of every atom and every land, mutually responding to one another. Here in this land, Śākyamuni manifests a body as an ordinary person to gather in those of his own kind;
through the capacity of a single atom and a single land, he unfolds the function of all atoms and lands.
That they do not see many and we do not see few is because the light of the six sense-gates of all sentient beings is identical to the single gate of Śākyamuni.
Their radiance intermingles and penetrates one another in infinite layers, like a banner of red pearls. Sentient beings do not know this;

they forget the entirety of the light and see only a single ray, regarding it as a marvelous sight. Śākyamuni knows this; he forgets the single ray and sees only the entirety of the light, regarding it with an impartial vision.
At that time, the world of Jambudvīpa and the Lotus-Flower-Pedestal Treasury World...
The realms are not two; Śākyamuni and Vairocana are not two bodies. All sentient beings, as numerous as motes of dust, are of no different nature from the Buddha upon the thousand-petaled lotus.
Thus, those who perceive the full-moon countenance [of the Buddha] all perceive the full-moon countenance.
Not only would Nāgasena cease his casting of the line, but even Vairocana himself would be forced to bind his tongue. Yet, this does not prevent one from forming a marvelous contemplation. Form it!
The Contemplation of Equality. Why is this? All Buddhas and sentient beings arise and perish in disorder;

this is precisely the Samādhi of the Body-Nature as Empty-Space Flower-Light. The Buddhas atop the thousand flowers are entirely contained within the Samādhi of the Body-Nature as Empty-Space Flower-Light.
Suddenly they manifest two times, suddenly they manifest two lands, and then they vanish into the Lotus-Womb Treasury beyond the realms, returning once more to the world of Jambudvīpa.
Having dissolved from the realms, he entered the Samādhi of the Body-Nature’s Flower-Light of Space.
Having emerged from the Samādhi of the Body-Nature’s Flower-Light of Space, prior to his dissolution and subsequent to his emergence, what kind of samādhi was it ultimately?
It was like a divine serpent that casts its own body, making it appear severed into inch-long pieces; once severed, it rejoins itself, leaving no trace whatsoever, even down to the finest atom.
The world, the Buddha, and sentient beings—separating and uniting, dispersing and gathering—are but a single divine serpent.
How could there be such a thing as the Samādhi of the Body-Nature of Empty Space, Flower Light? Or how could there be that which is not the Samādhi of the Body-Nature of Empty Space, Flower Light?

Furthermore, how could there be a time before entering the Samādhi of the Body-Nature of Empty Space, Flower Light, or a time after emerging from the Samādhi of the Body-Nature of Empty Space, Flower Light?
Arising from one's seat is the intrinsic purity of nature; this is precisely the essence of the unconditioned precept (*asaṃskṛta-śīla*). "Unconditioned" means simply not arising.
Vairocana did not arise from his majestic lion throne of celestial light, yet he manifested a thousand billion Śākyamunis, further transforming them without end.
The Buddha of Measurelessness sits within immeasurable lands, embracing immeasurable sentient beings; Vairocana never rises from his seat.
The hundreds of thousands of myriads of Śākyamunis are the very body of Vairocana, and all Jambudvīpas are the fundamental world of the Lotus-Womb Treasury (Padmagarbha).
To rise is, in truth, not to rise. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* manifests Śākyamuni as Vairocana, and for this reason [it does not speak of him rising].
He rose from his seat and preached the Dharma in ten locations. Because Vairocana manifests as Śākyamuni within the Brahma-net, he rises from his seat to preach the Dharma in ten locations.
Vairocana has the sense of non-arising, and Śākyamuni also has the sense of non-arising;
yet Śākyamuni has the sense of arising, and Vairocana also has the sense of arising. This is because Vairocana...
There is the meaning of arising; therefore, Śākyamuni manifests arising. Because Śākyamuni possesses the meaning of non-arising, Vairocana manifests non-arising.
In the daily activities of sentient beings, both of these two meanings are fully present: there is non-abiding in the conditioned, and non-abiding in the unconditioned.

Because it does not abide, it is called the "inherently pure Bodhisattva precept. Relying upon this, one does not abide in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), nor does one abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Śrāvaka is not so; therefore, the essence of the Śrāvaka precept is a distinct non-manifestation (*avijñapti*), whereas the essence of the Bodhisattva precept is...
One attains the Great Dhāraṇī,
the seed of the Buddha-nature,
the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. This was taught by Vairocana as the Buddha upon a thousand-petaled lotus, and it was received above by Maheśvara.

O Celestial One! Those ordinary beings below who are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance do not, however, obliterate the distinction between the sage and the ordinary person. Rather, the sage is the fruit of the ordinary person, and the ordinary person is the cause of the sage.
As an external record states: "In sacrificing at a river, one first honors the stream and later the sea; they share one source and flow into one mouth. This is what is meant by knowing the root.
Thus, how could the Buddhas of the three periods dare to forget all sentient beings of the three periods? Now, directly...
Vairocana constantly recites a single precept, which serves as the source of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. It is not yet known whether sentient beings take this precept as their own source;
otherwise, how would they differ from those who do not know their own origin? Now, the precept is not separately bound; it is bound in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*).

The Buddha is not separately accomplished; he is accomplished in accordance with the nature. If there were a separate cause, there would necessarily be a separate fruit. Since the precept [is the cause] for the Buddha...
Nature is the seed; therefore, it can give birth to Buddhas. Buddha-nature takes sentient beings as its seed; therefore, it can form sentient beings.
All sentient beings—whether they be of emotion or mind—enter the precepts of Buddha-nature like water entering water, or fire entering fire.
One perceives neither marks of difference nor marks of sameness, yet this does not obstruct the perception of difference, nor does it obstruct the perception of sameness. Why is this?
Therefore, when this is used to correspond with that, there are two types of correspondence: if they are identical in their capacity to correspond, then there is nothing to which it corresponds;

if they are different from that which is to be corresponded with, then there is likewise no capacity to correspond. Now, using the Buddha’s precepts to correspond with all sentient beings is like water entering water, because they correspond through the constant presence of the causal factor.
Using sentient beings to correspond with all the Buddha’s precepts is like fire entering fire, because they correspond through...

Because they abide eternally as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Since the Dharma-body is ever-present for sentient beings, there is no distinct cause. Sentient beings abide eternally; the Buddhas abide eternally. Originally, there is no distinct fruit.
The fruit corresponds to the cause; the cause corresponds to the fruit. The ordinary corresponds to the sage; the sage corresponds to the ordinary.

One should correspond to many; many should correspond to one. The present should correspond to the past; the past should correspond to the present. There are cases where two correspond, yet no case where one corresponds.

Therefore, there is no Buddha to be realized and no sentient beings to be saved. Because there is not even one correspondence that obstructs two correspondences, it is only for this reason that the precepts can be spoken.
The ten *pratimokṣas* appear in the world and are called the Dharma-precepts; they are also said to be used for discernment.
That which is non-dharma is, in fact, the Bodhisattva; yet in dharma there is no Bodhisattva. Sentient beings are not dharma; in dharma there are no sentient beings.

Dharma is the precept of non-dharma; non-dharma is the precept of dharma. Thus have the Buddhas of the three periods of time spoken—spoken initially, spoken repeatedly, and spoken by the hundreds, thousands, and billions.
One cannot become a distinct Buddha apart from the self-nature of sentient beings; likewise, one cannot establish a distinct precept apart from the self-nature of sentient beings.
It is simply called the "precept of all sentient beings. Sentient beings have no room for yielding, and the Buddha has no expression of self-importance;
sentient beings likewise have no expression of self-importance, and the Buddha likewise has no room for yielding. Why is this? Because all Buddhas are... all [sentient beings].
The Bodhisattva originates from the purity of self-nature; the Buddha is its ocean, and sentient beings are its rivers. They share one source and flow into one confluence.
This is what is meant by "knowing the root. Therefore it is said that the Buddha is the mother of sentient beings, and sentient beings are likewise the mother of the Buddha.
The Buddha is the teacher of sentient beings, and sentient beings are also the teachers of the Buddha. Sentient beings receive and uphold the Buddha’s nature-precepts upon their heads;
the Buddha’s precepts, which are intrinsically pure, are likewise received and upheld by all sentient beings upon their heads.
Thus, sentient beings repay the Buddha’s kindness, and the Buddha also repays the kindness of sentient beings.
In the Śrāvaka Vinaya of the tenfold categories of precepts,

there are both natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) and prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*). The four *pārājika* offenses are called natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), because they exist within the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
There is an offense. It is not that the Buddha’s formulation of the precepts was the first to prohibit it; therefore, all others are *pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya* (prohibited offenses).

In the Mahāyāna, for this reason, among the ten grave offenses (*daśa-śīla*), the first four are considered *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherent offenses). This accords with the meaning of the "mind-ground" (*citta-bhūmi*).

Now, as for what is called "innate purity" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), if one does not even cling to the stains of the wholesome or the defiled, how much less would one cling to the stains of evil? Thus, since the nature itself is without nature, how could there be any offense?
When one searches for the nature of transgression within, without, or in between, it cannot be found. How could there possibly be a nature of transgression?

All sentient beings accomplish karmic transgressions through greed, hatred, and delusion; these are merely habitual tendencies. Habitual tendency is the cause of transgression, and transgression is the fruit of habitual tendency.

The nature of cause and effect is such that there is the nature of cultivation and non-cultivation, and the nature of transgression and non-transgression; how much more so regarding their inherent nature (*prakṛti*)?

If one were to claim that other offenses only become offenses through the prohibitions of the Vinaya, then even without the Vinaya, they would not constitute offenses. This is because [the Buddha] intentionally entered [the world], and thus it is a fault of his own making.
Now, as for what is called a "natural precept" (*prakṛti-śīla*), all minor precepts are also natural precepts, because they are able to obstruct the [innate] nature.
Because it prevents [the nature] from manifesting, its nature is thus obstructed; this is called "nature-precept" (*prakṛti-śīla*).

In fact, all precepts possess the meaning of "nature. Others do not elaborate on this. For example, when a lay follower (*upāsaka*) breaks even one precept by drinking alcohol, all four precepts are thereby destroyed;
therefore, these are called "prohibitive precepts" (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*). Thus, all grave offenses are prohibitive precepts, for they likewise obstruct the nature and prevent it from manifesting.
To prohibit and prevent is called "prohibitive precepts" (*pratikṣepa-śīla*). This refers to all precepts, as they all possess the meaning of prohibition. Others need not be discussed further;

it is also like the case of an upāsaka, who, by drinking even a single measure of alcohol, breaks all four precepts. Thus, the Tathāgata’s formulation of precepts does not exceed the purpose of prohibition.
As for those things that constitute natural obstructions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), their nature is originally not sinful; rather, it is the obstruction itself that has varying degrees of depth. And...
Regarding the prohibition of initial transgressions, there are degrees of gravity. All precepts are prohibitory precepts, and thus they are all natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*).

However, one cannot call them "natural offenses" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), as that would contradict their essential purity (*svabhāva-viśuddhi*). Therefore, those who study the Mahāyāna should not fail to distinguish themselves from the Śrāvakas.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "To obstruct the continuity of future [rebirth] is called 'killing. What the Bodhisattvas do is to emerge from and submerge back into the ocean of birth and death.
When Śrāvakas enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), they scorch the sprout of the Buddha and destroy the seed of the Buddha; for this, the Buddha rebukes them."
"It is only fitting that he be an evil person.
A bhikṣu, practicing the contemplation of impurity, became weary of his body and committed suicide. This was the beginning of the Śrāvakas' formulation of the precepts."
The Bodhisattva, however, sacrifices his own body. For a Śrāvaka, killing a human being constitutes a grave offense (pārājika), while killing an animal is a *pāyattika*.
Yet, if a Bodhisattva perceives that an icchantika intends to harm many sentient beings or intends to destroy the True Dharma, he may give rise to great compassion and take its life.
Furthermore, while a Śrāvaka may eat the five kinds of pure meat, a Bodhisattva does not eat them; he does not even keep implements for killing or engage in trade involving them.
To sell instruments of killing—if this were so, one would rather kill a human than a beast. A human has a transgression for which they may be killed; a beast has no such transgression.

Among beasts there is neither great nor small: during the causal stage of his practice, Śākyamuni Buddha manifested in the body of a louse, and Devadatta was nearly harmed by being pulled along by a mere earth flea.
With the eye of the Path, a Bodhisattva observes with equality that there is not even a speck of a sentient being who is not [a potential Buddha].
Regarding the seed of Buddha-nature: Buddha-nature cannot be severed, and thus its future continuity likewise cannot be severed.

When this aggregate perishes and that aggregate arises, who is there to act as a killer? Yet, since there exists the precept against killing, it is appropriate to both permit and prohibit according to whether an action is good or evil.
When a Bodhisattva does not sever the future continuity, they do not sever the continuity of goodness, yet they do sever [the continuity of] evil.
The continuity of evil persists; as long as this continuity of evil is not severed, the continuity of goodness is severed.

When goodness is severed, the cause for generating the bodhicitta is severed, and the fruit of attaining equal and perfect enlightenment is severed. Therefore, there is no sin in killing an icchantika.

Although an icchantika does not sever their buddha-nature, they do sever their roots of goodness. An animal possesses some roots of goodness; thus, there is sin in killing one. This is with respect to a single thought-moment.

The point of origination. Discerning and opening. Discerning and obstructing. Discerning the severance of function. Discerning the continuity of function. Discerning the function of the three periods of time.
The non-obstruction of the continuity of the three periods of time. Discerning the non-obstruction of continuity. Non-obstructing continuity yet being decisive.
Decisively obstructing the evil continuity of the future. Continuing the virtuous continuity of the future. Until [enlightenment] is attained.
The Buddha himself acted in this way; he taught others to act likewise.
To take what is not given is called theft. Since all phenomena (dharmas) have no giver, how could one take them? Yet now, you simply take them.
"Unsurpassed Bodhi. As for this unsurpassed Bodhi, who bestows it? Does heaven bestow it? Does earth bestow it?
Do parents, teachers, or the Sangha bestow it? Does the Buddha bestow it? Since there is no one who bestows it, then whoever thinks they take it is a thief.
The thousand Buddhas extend their hands; they specifically extend their hands and say: 'You raise your hand and I shall give it to you. Lu [Hanshan]...
Vairocana has hands; the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis have hands; and immeasurable sentient beings also have hands.
Those hands give nothing, and these hands take nothing. To give while there is nothing given is likewise theft.
Sentient beings do not steal from the Buddha; the Buddha does not steal from sentient beings. Vairocana does not steal from Śākyamuni; Śākyamuni does not steal from Vairocana.
All Bodhisattvas do not steal from those who have attained Buddhahood to save sentient beings; all sentient beings do not steal from those who practice the Bodhisattva path to attain Buddhahood.

To abandon birth and death while committing killing; to grasp at nirvana while committing theft; to abandon greed, hatred, and delusion while committing killing; to grasp at precepts, concentration, and wisdom while committing theft;
to abandon the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span while committing killing; to grasp at the non-existence of self, person, sentient being, and life-span while committing theft;
to abandon grasping and non-grasping while committing killing; and to grasp at neither grasping nor abandoning while committing theft.
When wicked people usurp great positions and seize great names, taking by force things that are not rightfully theirs, the Bodhisattva employs skillful means to take them away.
Those who previously claimed such things as their own are left utterly destitute; only then do they realize these were not theirs to possess. Thus does the Bodhisattva take them away.
Nor do they belong to oneself; it is simply emptiness uniting with emptiness. All things have no master, yet because sentient beings possess a self, they appear to have a master.
While the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) rages, the principle of ownership and its momentum cannot be transgressed;
they are all like ghosts and spirits, or like bandits. Regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), whatever one grasps—whether much or little—is but a single [delusion].
Every blade of grass is a needle; every needle is a blade of grass. Just as every blade of grass is a needle, so too are all material possessions.
A Bodhisattva seizes them all, likening them to the impermanence of the four great elements; there is not a single kṣaṇa in which they are not seized.
Yet people remain bold and arrogant, thinking, "I have a master. When the light of their eyes falls to the ground, even "I" has no master—how much less so that which belongs to me?
There is. Is it not perhaps that one unites emptiness with emptiness? Yet those whose habituation to robbery is profound fall further into the realm of ghosts and spirits;
thus, the Bodhisattva is able to steal from thieves, only then beginning to be without theft. However, it is only by being without theft that one can truly steal from thieves.
A novice monk eavesdropped on the *poṣadha* ceremony; the Śrāvakas did not grant him full ordination (*upasampadā*), yet this was not prohibited for a Bodhisattva.
Since phenomena have no inherent existence, he had merely stolen emptiness. Once, at Dongshan, there were ninety-six turning words;
one monk listened in secret but could not grasp the very last word. He served [the master] as an attendant for three years, yet in the end, it was never explained to him.
When he was ill, someone took his belongings by force with a knife. If a Bodhisattva were to see this, he would first grant him a reward. Why is this?
Because that monk’s final words concerned even a single needle or a blade of grass; yet that person, with a mind of grasping, guarded it and seized it from him.
And yet it is empty. This is because one uses a mind that seeks attainment to grasp at attainment, and then empties it again; this is merely the meeting of two aspects of attainment.
Lust.
Craving is lust; grasping is theft. Lust involves internal forms and external forms. Seeking from others constitutes the external; seeking within oneself constitutes the internal.
To seek, to obtain, and to dwell upon these are all the karma of lust. A Bodhisattva does not dwell upon forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects while practicing giving.
Giving is the excellent medicine for lust; not dwelling [upon sense objects] is the fundamental prescription for giving.
All women, even down to those among the animals, and the daughters of devas and ghosts—these are the phenomena of the six realms and the three worlds.

Mothers, daughters, and sisters—these are the phenomena of the six kinships across the three periods of time. To transcend the Way and emerge from the twenty-five states of existence, and to leave behind birth and extinction to dwell in the dharma of quiescent extinction.
"I have a wife whom no one in the world has ever seen; morning and evening she stays with me, and naturally there are expedient means [between us].
Old Wuzu has for a time slipped into the ranks of the laypeople. If you can send away this old woman, the business of your lifelong study will be finished."

Sentient beings are fundamentally pure. To say now that "pure dharmas are given to people" is merely because those who love what is impure are shown that there are pure dharmas, and those who love purity are shown that there are dharmas to be given;
this too is but the skillful means of a bodhisattva’s intentional falsehood.
False speech may be pure or defiled; it may involve gain or loss; it may have arising and ceasing, or going and coming; it may be permanent or impermanent;
it may be one or different—all these are false speech. To say one has seen what was not seen, or to say one has not seen what was seen, is false speech. To say one has seen...

If one sees but says they do not see, is that not ultimately false speech? Only when one recognizes seeing as "not seeing" and non-seeing as "seeing" can one truly say that what is seen is seen and what is not seen is not seen.
The body is the substance of delusion; the mind is the name of delusion. Body and mind are thus false speech. To know that body and mind are false speech is to be without body or mind.
To perceive body and mind within this state of no-body-and-no-mind, yet speak of body and mind—this is called right speech and right view.
A bodhisattva has the false speech of a bodhisattva, and a śrāvaka has the false speech of a śrāvaka; these must not be confused with one another.
When a bodhisattva first generates the resolve for enlightenment, they believe that they and all sentient beings have already attained buddhahood.

If such a person says to others, "I have already become a buddha," there is no offense, because it is done to inspire in sentient beings a superior sense of responsibility and burden. [If, however,] for the sake of fame, profit, or gain, they manifest...

Regarding the characteristic of deception, the gravity of the offense of false speech is determined by the following: although he has not yet attained [the fruits], he originally possessed them and thus has not lost them;

furthermore, this is not a "great false speech," because the Buddha is inherent in all sentient beings and is not something external. If one says that he has attained the four fruits or that devas and nāgas have come, [it constitutes a grave offense].
To claim that ghosts and spirits have come is an inferior and false statement. A Bodhisattva will ultimately attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime;

to abandon the Great [Vehicle] and preach the Small [Vehicle] would how could it be fit to incur a grave offense? To cite the example of the Śrāvakas to establish a grave offense for this one case contradicts the original aspiration of the Bodhisattva.
If the causal ground were not broad, then because of this one person, one should not disparage all Bodhisattvas. This is the first point.
First among those who sell wine, one must not sell the "wine of the Dharma of Samādhi. This is a lethal poison for Bodhisattvas.
Since the Śrāvakas have already drunk it themselves, how can they possibly compare to those who sell it to others?

There is a Buddha who can be realized; there are sentient beings who can be delivered; there is a Dharma that can be taught. If a Bodhisattva commits this offense of selling liquor, it is treated according to the same precedent as for Śrāvakas.
There are currently those who recite the precepts: Śākyamuni acted as a bridge and a ferry for delivering sentient beings and realizing Buddhahood.
Furthermore, by what analogy could one say that once all sentient beings have already attained Buddhahood, already completed the deliverance of beings, and already entered nirvana,
the thousand billion Śākyamunis will then take their thousand billion wines and expect you to have long since demolished [the house]?

To speak of the faults of the fourfold assembly is itself a fault. Since they have already committed a fault, what more is there to say? If this is so, why then are the ten grave precepts and forty-eight light precepts taught?
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Not abiding is called a guest; abiding is called the host. Faults possess the quality of being a guest. [Bodhi]...
In the *Saddharmacittabhūmi*, there is the principle of the permanently abiding (*nitya-sthita*). Whether good comes or evil comes, both are guests; guests are not permanently abiding.

That which is permanently abiding does not receive blame from the guest, for the permanently abiding is not the guest. Nor does the guest produce blame for the permanently abiding, for the guest is not the permanently abiding.

Nevertheless, in the way a host treats a guest, there is a proper way: the host distinguishes the guest and further distinguishes the permanently abiding, merely causing them to recognize their faults. Merely...
He causes them to repent their transgressions, yet does not speak of their faults, because he regards them as guests rather than as permanent residents.

Guests may possess what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya, yet they may also possess Dharma and Vinaya; permanent residents, however, possess neither Dharma nor Vinaya, nor do they possess what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya.
That wicked person, while using what is neither Dharma nor Vinaya to cast doubt upon the host, fails to realize that it is the Dharma and Vinaya which constitute the guest. The Bodhisattva...
If one explains this erroneously, causing others to lose their wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna, they will ultimately fail to recognize the eternal abiding (nitya-dharmatā) and become icchantikas.
Since icchantikas fail to recognize the eternal abiding, yet the eternal abiding exists, the eternal abiding is neither at fault nor without fault.
The fault of the icchantika cannot even be described; how much less so the faults of the Bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly?

Self-praise and disparaging others do not involve a self that is separate from others, nor a "other" that is separate from oneself. If one were to say that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is the self and conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) is the other;

that intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) is the self and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are the other; or that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the self and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is the other—all such cases constitute self-praise.

To disparage others is to direct evil toward oneself; to praise others is to bestow goodness upon them. Furthermore, to praise oneself while disparaging others is to place the fruit of evil upon another—how could that be directed toward oneself?

And to place the fruit of goodness upon oneself—how could that be bestowed upon another? When sentient beings perceive the evils of other sentient beings, the Bodhisattva perceives only their goodness.
Since verbal praise is insufficient, one should instead apply oneself to prostrations toward sentient beings.
As for those who bring insult and humiliation, it is not only the Bodhisattva who receives them; fundamentally, they are of one body, and thus the Buddhas of the three periods receive them as well.
There is originally no dual body to act as a substitute. To speak of "substituting" is still a matter of being obstructed by a barrier.
The Bodhisattva manifests the marks of all sentient beings, while sentient beings manifest the marks of all Buddhas; such is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

It is not a matter of withdrawing oneself or yielding to others by saying, "I shall attain Buddhahood, but you shall not. To say this is to conceal the good qualities of others and cause them to suffer disparagement.
Even if one were to say, "Even if I attain Buddhahood, you too shall attain Buddhahood," it remains a concealment of another's good qualities.
Causing others to suffer humiliation;

out of stinginess and envy, he further reviles this person who is as wealthy as the entire earth, appearing without cause in the guise of a beggar. The Bodhisattva [bestowed] the deity within the lining of his robe.

The pearl. To offer a golden pitcher for the consecration is something one possesses inherently; it is common to all people. To give rise to the view of "I" and bestow it upon another is itself an act of either enhancement or disparagement.
How much more so when one is stingy and begrudges its equal distribution? A starving person does not eat food offered with a "Come here!"—this too is within the scope of seeking [alms].
The family tradition of the wealthy and prosperous should give rise to a sense of shame regarding the display of virtue.

The entire earth is a pauper, yet they do not know the wondrousness of poverty. If such a person suddenly comes to beg from a Bodhisattva, and the Bodhisattva gives them even a small teaching, it would be as if one were killing their life.
Not to speak a single word or a single verse, nor to give even a speck of dust’s worth of Dharma—this may be called being a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
I permit him to revile all beggars; for the Sūtra does not [say otherwise].
I fear that last year you had no land and this year you have not even a needle; yet you have still not reached such a state.
Even if you truly reach such a state, you must still go begging before you can attain it.

Regarding anger and the refusal of repentance, the *Teaching Left Behind* (Yizhiao) states: "Within clear and cool clouds, for lightning to produce fire is not what is appropriate. This means that within clear and cool clouds, there is no obstruction to lightning producing fire;
it is simply that this is not the permanent nature of things. Lightning-fire is not the permanent nature of things, yet within the clear and cool [clouds], it occurs.
Clouds, too, are not permanent phenomena. When one harbors anger and does not understand this, how can one know that this unresolvable anger perishes moment by moment?
Anger perishes moment by moment; the words of abuse perish word by word; the blows perish stroke by stroke. One who abuses does not see the striking;

one who is struck does not hear the abuse. The mouth is unaware of the hand; the hand is unaware of the blade or staff; the blade or staff is unaware of the anger; and the anger is unaware of the thought.
Thoughts arise and perish; each thought perishing moment by moment is unaware of itself. Yet, there remains an inexplicable anger—this is what is called the "inexplicable.
All sentient beings are, in truth, not sentient beings. There is no need to further employ emotional sympathy, nor is there need to further employ rational dismissal.

Who is the one who feels anger? Who is the object of that anger? The one who feels anger manifests the appearance of a sentient being; the one who has apologized manifests the appearance of a non-sentient being.

Those who appear as non-sentient beings are those who do not recognize the anger of others as being non-sentient. Those who appear as sentient beings are those who do not recognize the gratitude of others as being non-sentient.
If one attains [this realization], both are attained; if one loses it, both are lost.
There are also bodhisattvas who do not accept remorse. This is because they do not know that the nature of transgression is ungraspable.
Such a person merely regrets what is unwholesome; it is not that the bodhisattva does not accept remorse. There is no way to receive a transgression. Why?
Because there is no place for a transgression to be received, and likewise no place for remorse to be received. This is called wholesome regret and wholesome acceptance.

To slander the Triple Gem is to say that the Triple Gem is not something else; the eternally abiding Buddha-nature is it. That the eternally abiding Buddha-nature is not something else is the mind of all sentient beings.
To seek the Triple Gem outside of the mind is called being a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). To abandon sentient beings within the Triple Gem is called...

Regarding the two vehicles and evil persons who slander the Buddha: for a Bodhisattva, such slandering minds are like thorns piercing the heart. To say "sentient beings are the Buddha" is the slander of superimposition (*samāropa*).
To say "sentient beings are not the Buddha" is the slander of deprecation (*apavāda*). To say "they both are and are not" is the slander of contradiction (*virodha*).
To say "they neither are nor are not" is the slander of frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
The mind takes slander as its meaning; taking sentient beings as the mind is itself slandering sentient beings;
taking the Triple Gem as the mind is itself slandering the Triple Gem; taking that which is neither sentient beings nor the Triple Gem as the mind is itself slandering the mind.
Thus, everything is slandered, and yet the whole mind alone is revealed. When a Bodhisattva can slander in this manner, it is called "non-slandering."

Maitreya said: "To slander the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and to preach counterfeit teachings with fervent persistence—this is what is meant in the *Laṅkāvatāra* by 'having first accepted the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion, and subsequently, through false conceptualization and attachment, declaring that the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is non-nature.
The extinction of the Buddha-dharma truly arises from this precept; therefore, it is called 'rescue. If one takes the mere upholding [of these words] as the true Dharma, then..."
The dharma of resemblance: taking that which is without reception and without grasping as the true dharma is also a dharma of resemblance;
taking that which is not a true dharma as the true dharma is also a dharma of resemblance.
Regarding the ten grave precepts for teaching others, each is first committed by oneself; second is teaching others. This is the primary focus of the Bodhisattva’s instruction.

As for the distinction between light and heavy within these acts of teaching others, it is incorrect to say that fame and profit are grave when they pertain to oneself but light when they pertain to others. For the Bodhisattva saves all sentient beings.
This constitutes the foremost matter. To teach others unwholesome dharmas is to damage the foremost practice, to violate the foremost vow, and to directly destroy the foremost precept;
how could one have leisure to inquire whether fame and profit reside in oneself or in others? Furthermore, a bodhisattva would rather break their own precepts themselves.
One will fall into hell. One certainly cannot bear to sit idly by while another breaks the precepts and falls into hell;

yet, it would be better for one's own reputation and profit to remain intact while another commits a grave offense, rather than for one's own reputation and profit to be lost while one merely commits a minor offense.

All of these [arguments] rely on the Vinaya of the Hīnayāna to interpret the Mahāyāna, thereby missing the Buddha’s original intent. Furthermore, it is said that the first four grave matters are equivalent to the seven [offenses].
[The first four] are prohibitions; both regret and lack of regret constitute obstacles. Regarding the latter six, regret is not an obstacle, whereas lack of regret is an obstacle. Some say:

for the first four, it is necessary to feel regret, and seeing their characteristics does not constitute an obstacle; for the latter six, even lacking regret does not constitute an obstacle. The Buddha taught the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of the Chapter on Precepts; initially, there is no distinction.
However, when discussing the Bodhisattva path, the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) establishes the first four as prohibitions within its own domain.
The Lesser Vehicle is narrow and coarse; the Mahāyāna regulations for the latter six [categories] are broad and subtle within the classification of persons.

If one emphasizes the instruction of people, then if one does not instruct them to repent their offenses, how could they be classified as light? It is said: In those cases, the person already possesses an offense;
if one does not instruct them to repent, it is light. In this case, there was originally no offense; because one instructs them to commit it, it is heavy.
Regarding the precept on maintaining the Dharma with an evil mind, one must first examine the causal ground. As the Sūtra states, "an evil mind" refers to any state of mind that is inherently evil.

A mind set on self-benefit is the pursuit of gain and offerings; a mind set on benefiting others is the pursuit of fame and reputation; and a mind that seeks after or grasps at anything is likewise an evil mind.

Regarding gain and offerings: when there is a mind that seeks nothing and attains nothing, this is [the state of] fame. When there is a mind, one transgresses; when there is no mind, one maintains [the precepts].
This is the stage of original self-nature purity. Where there is [a mind], there is defilement. Because one desires to receive, one grasps; once grasped, one receives.
For a Bodhisattva, regarding all phenomena, one first cuts off receiving. One does not receive anything at all, yet it is not a matter of cutting off receiving.

To lose one's position and commit a grave transgression is to lose all positions, even unto the loss of all sublime fruits. It does not say that the bodhicitta is lost, for bodhicitta is something that cannot be lost.
Therefore, it says that one cannot manifest the arousal of bodhicitta in this present body; it means that one is unable to arouse it.

It is not that the bodhicitta is absent; yet one falls into the three evil realms. Who is it that falls? It is those who have not heard the names of their parents or the Three Jewels. Who is it that does not hear them?
When one turns the light back for even a single thought-moment, the entire body passes through and out. Only then does one realize that from within hell, one has gone directly to Tuṣita Heaven.

Hearing the sound of the celestial drum, one immediately realizes the ten stages (bhūmis). Fundamentally, there is no gradual progression; therefore, the precepts of the Śrāvakas [are but a partial measure].
There is gain and loss; however, the Bodhisattva precepts have neither gain nor loss. Because the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding, it is neither gained nor lost.
Thus, even those icchantikas all receive the prediction of enlightenment, for they neither gain faith nor lose their lack of faith.
After forty-eight minor transgressions, one fails to respect teachers and friends.
That which cannot be seen in the teacher is the Buddha-nature; that which can be seen in the teacher consists of the Upādhyāya and the Ācārya.
Those who do not act as my companions are my teachers. Those who act as my companions are fellow students, fellow practitioners, and those of like view.
By following my companions, I perceive that which they do not; by following what is visible, I attain that which is invisible. How could I dare not revere them?
Those who wish to receive my teaching must empty themselves of all possessions: their bodies, kingdoms, cities, wives, children, the seven treasures, and all manner of goods.

"I dare not fail to sell them. To purchase them specifically is like marrying a worm; knowing there is no owner to whom they can be sold, even a single needle or a blade of grass must not be retained.
This is what constitutes true Dharma-offering."

Having heard that all sentient beings possess the eternally abiding Buddha-nature, one who drinks [this teaching] yet follows the deluded thoughts and mental fluxes of sentient beings is like a drunkard.
The vessels for holding the wine include the *lei* and the *zun*; the vessels for drawing the wine include the *bei* and the *shao*. All of these are metaphors for the dharmas of reception.
Among those who have transcended humanity, there are those who grasp at phenomena; they do not realize that there is neither wine nor a vessel.
How could one who has not lived for five hundred lifetimes know that there is no hand?

A Bodhisattva who "eats meat" may kill yet not consume it; for "eating" carries the meaning of "utilization. One who kills greed, hatred, and delusion will certainly never utilize greed, hatred, and delusion.
One who kills ignorance and afflictions will certainly never utilize ignorance and afflictions.
The Bodhisattva has that which nourishes yet does not eat. He nourishes the six perfections, yet there is no one who enjoys the six perfections;
he nourishes the ten thousand practices, yet there is no one who enjoys the ten thousand practices. For this reason, the Bodhisattva does not receive food; food is merely meat.

Regarding those who consume the five pungent roots while practicing the methods for cultivating the mind-ground: if they possess even a slight trace of the breath of the Bodhisattva path, they have already violated the prohibition against the five pungent roots;
how much more so when they fatten themselves by eating the "meat of merit" and become intoxicated by drinking the "wine of precepts, concentration, and supernormal powers"?
While it is not permitted for a Bodhisattva who has not been instructed to repent their transgressions to speak of them, it is permitted to raise the matter of their offenses.

This is because if one neither raises the matter nor causes repentance, it would cause all sentient beings to remain forever within the state of sinful dharmas. That sinful dharmas do not remain permanent is precisely what prevents the constant loss of those sinful dharmas.
The meaning of "permanently abiding" (nitya) is precisely the loss of the meaning of the permanent abiding of Buddha-nature.
To be born before a Buddha or after a Buddha constitutes one of the eight difficulties (aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ). Why, then, is it called being "before or after a Buddha"?

It refers to sentient beings who do not believe that they themselves are Buddhas; to pass by face-to-face [the opportunity for enlightenment] is what is meant by being "before or after a Buddha. The other seven difficulties all stem from this one.
It is difficult for one to be born [as a Buddha]. Some say that since the Buddha has already appeared in this world, it is best to repent of one's transgressions from time to time.
If one holds such a view, one must wait until Maitreya’s descent to be born again, which is still separated by three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

A Bodhisattva who does not provide for others when requested to teach the Dharma has three kinds of spiritual friends: the primary teacher-friend, the circumstantial teacher-friend, and the universal teacher-friend.
These are called circumstantial teacher-friends because they involve coming and going. That which is called the Mahāyāna Dharma is able to digest all food.
Those who study the Mahāyāna Dharma are able to extinguish all bodies and are able to digest all food; therefore, they are worthy of offerings.
Because they can extinguish all bodies, they are worthy of prostration. If this is so, then between the Dharma master and the one who invites the Dharma master—
It preaches the Dharma at all times; how could it be limited to only three periods?

Even when one is indolent and does not listen to the Dharma, wherever the Vinaya and Sūtras are being expounded, that alone is the sounding of the celestial drum—yet no one understands or listens to it.
As for those who understand and can listen, whether it be a noisy place or a quiet one, a nearby location or a distant one— whichever place the Dharma Master proclaims [the teaching],
simply take what you have mastered from the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Abhidharma to that spot for a single verification. If you do not yet understand how to listen, then for the time being,
receive the instruction directly before the high seat.

To turn one's back on the Great and face the Small is for the whole mind to become the Mahāyāna of the eternally abiding sūtras and vinayas. When the Buddha spoke of these as the entirety, the mind suddenly arises and turns its back;
it does not realize that this very turning away is itself the mind. While bearing the burden upon one shoulder, one still does not accept or uphold the Mahāyāna of the eternally abiding [teachings].
Regarding the sutras and vinayas, how could one further uphold those of the Two Vehicles or the evil views of external paths? Alas! To believe in this is truly not easy.
Having no other choice, I permit their coming and going; yet only a Buddha can endure such vexation and difficulty. Nevertheless, it is not a matter of enduring vexation:
with a single somersault, one travels eighty thousand miles, never leaving the palm of the Tathāgata’s hand.
To tend to all sick people as if they were the Buddha, and to regard all Buddhas as if they were sick people—this is to be a great king of physicians.
What are meant by parents, teachers, monks, and disciples? It is when their faculties are incomplete; these are the hundred kinds of illnesses.
The illness upon arriving home is the fundamental illness. What are called monasteries, cities, wildernesses, mountain forests, and the illnesses encountered on the road?
These are the illnesses before arriving home; they are the secondary and peripheral illnesses. The secondary and peripheral [illnesses] cause one to recognize the fundamental;

those before arriving home lead to arriving home—this is the method of salvation. The fundamental causes the secondary and peripheral to arise; arriving home causes one to depart from the gate—this is the offering.
The practice of nurturing is the law of killing sentient beings.

Whether the instruments for killing are permanent or impermanent, whether they are "self" or "non-self," whether they are "liberation" or "non-liberation"— all such signs of discordance and unrest are the very breath of killing.
Furthermore, whether it be the Dharma or non-Dharma, the Vinaya or non-Vinaya, upholding or violating—these are all instruments of killing. What harm is there in possessing them?

One need only eliminate the two views. When the Bodhisattva Padma deployed his great four-sided net to capture sentient beings, he did not ensnare their feet. The swords, staves, bows, and arrows were all released together.
The Bodhisattva’s Grounds are like those of a Wheel-Turning Sage King; no other minor kings dare to oppose his countenance in their conduct, nor can any other minor kings act as his companions.
Now, for two such kingdoms to raise armies and strike one another is the Dharma of Antidotes.
That the lowest [of beings] would willingly serve as a messenger for a Bodhisattva can be called a perverted view.

The messenger serves as a messenger for one nation, while the thief acts as a thief for two nations; this is because they establish distinctions within a single Dharma-realm, thereby killing immeasurable sentient beings.
One hopes to achieve the Buddha-way; yet the Buddha-way will certainly not be achieved. Not only does one plunder sentient beings, but one also plunders the Buddha.
Therefore it is said: "Luminosity and non-luminosity—fools perceive them as two; the wise realize that their nature is non-dual. This nature of non-duality—
This is precisely the true nature.

Those who trade in noble persons are the fundamental nature; those who are slaves are the six sense faculties; and those who are domestic animals are the six sense objects. [They] have been brought here for sale.

To sell it away and suppress the noble to become base is the seed of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), which is like placing a corpse inside a coffin. To slander and destroy [the Dharma] is the seed of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
All sentient beings are, from the beginning, without affairs; that is to say, they are noble persons and virtuous people.

Dharma masters, teachers, and monks, kings, and nobles are fundamentally the fourfold assembly and the three bodies. The six relations are fundamentally the dharmas of the three periods of time. Their present activities manifest within the three periods, yet fundamentally they do not combine with any causes or conditions.
Though they flow into the five paths, they are fundamentally unstained. Within this, there is not even [a single thing].

Regarding those who do not commit the seven reversals or the ten grave offenses: how could there be anyone who commits the seven reversals or the ten grave offenses, yet claims that another has committed them?
This is merely groundless slander against others. Within the great void, there is no color to be painted and no poison to be smeared;
yet those with evil minds perceive themselves as inflicting harm and falling into undesirable states. It is not so.

To know that within the state of fundamental non-action, the mind of filial piety and the mind of compassion are placed in a state of "as-it-is" (yìrúchù)—all these are matters of excessive activity (*bahukṛtya*).
When setting fire to burn things, each has its own basis, like a viper clinging to its burrow. The Bodhisattva burns it with a great fire so that one may see clearly and suddenly.

The realm of the power of the white bones (*śvetāsthi*) is the skillful means for this liberation. If one pursues movement, one becomes attached to the contemplation of mountains, forests, and wilderness;
wait until they enter these, and burn them. If one guards stillness, one becomes attached to dwelling in human homes or monastic quarters;
wait until they emerge from these, and burn them. They emerge and then re-enter, yet no place of their abiding is seen. They enter and then re-emerge, yet no object of their observation is seen.
Thus, skillful means are accomplished. A skilled physician uses medicine to eliminate the disease without harming the eye;
an unskilled physician loses both the eye and the medicine—burning that which is expelled at the time of exit and burning that which is introduced at the time of entry. This is what is meant.
At times the Bodhisattva destroys the world; at times he creates the world. At times he gives everything away;
at times he takes everything away. Taking and giving are both given; creation and destruction are both created.
From biased teachings to the Buddha’s own disciples, from non-Buddhist heretics and wicked people to one's own six relations—all are universal spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Throughout the entire earth, there is not even so much as a single hair’s breadth of an evil friend. Therefore, the entirety of the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas is beyond words.
This is the characteristic of the written word. To believe in this is called "arousing the bodhicitta. To practice this is called the "sequential application of the Dharma.
Sentient beings encounter conditions for untimely death—dying when they ought not to die.

It is like being on a straight, open road where all directions are clear, only to be suddenly led by someone into a circuitous, perilous, and evil path, becoming one who meets with an untimely death. This is what is meant.
An evil mind or a mind of anger cannot be found therein. Nevertheless, that is not an evil mind nor a mind of anger; this, too, is not an untimely death.
One realizes that all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) have been fundamentally upon the thorough, open road all along.
Bai Le taught his favorite disciple how to appraise ordinary horses, while he taught his least-favored disciple how to appraise horses of a thousand li.

Ordinary horses were common and thus sold; horses of a thousand li were rare and thus did not sell. Now, if one does not know how to appraise ordinary horses, how can they appraise horses of a thousand li?
And if one is already able to recognize horses of a thousand li, how could they fail to recognize ordinary horses? Thus it was with Bai Le.
Joy is not hindered by likes or dislikes; it is only his disciples who are obstructed by ordinary horses and "thousand-li" steeds.
Those of the Two Vehicles seek the thousand-li steed outside of horses, while the non-Buddhists take ordinary horses to be the thousand-li steeds.
Even those who attain their celestial faculty beyond the black or yellow of mares and stallions have never attained it within the company of deer or swine.
For the sake of benefiting others, he explains that the entire dharma-realm is of this single nature. This single nature is the True Dharma; the True Dharma is the Three Jewels.

Because the view of a self-body gives rise to obstructions, [the Dharma] does not manifest before one. Therefore, one should burn one’s body, arms, and fingers as an offering to the Buddhas, and sacrifice one’s own flesh, hands, and feet.
To feed hungry tigers, wolves, lions, and all hungry ghosts, one need only have a resolute mind; they will certainly not deceive you.
If it is said that tigers, wolves, and lions do not understand how to preach the Dharma, [the Master] says: "The Buddhas themselves do not understand how to preach the Dharma.
"If so, where should one seek [the Dharma]? "Seek it right within yourself. I have already abandoned my body; whom else would I teach to seek it? "If you do not abandon [yourself]," [he asks].
Body. Who taught you to seek it?
To prosper in the world, one must first eliminate harm. This is not yet to understand the meaning of sequential order. When a Bodhisattva eliminates harm, he does so by first eliminating benefit;
this is what is meant by "having before" and "having after. When the Goddess of Merit arrives, the Woman of Darkness likewise arrives. There is...
The wise master accepts neither of these two; only then does the mind open and the intellect attain liberation.

Relying on one's power to beg from kings, princes, ministers, and officials—who possess the marks of respect due to the Triple Gem—is not to seek the Buddha through attachment, nor is it to be attached [to them].
