Seeking the Dharma without attachment to the Sangha is true intimacy. To have something to seek as one's intimacy, and to rely on that intimacy for support, is to be a hired laborer.
When one investigates the internal, external, and intermediate, there is the manifestation of the aspect of begging;

when one cuts off arising and ceasing, there is the manifestation of the aspect of beating; at all times, when one exerts control, there is the manifestation of the aspect of dragging and pulling. There is...
To grasp at existence is to obtain; it is like a poor man suddenly becoming wealthy, manifesting the appearance of seizing wealth by force. This is the Dharma of non-attainment.
What, then, is there to seek? To have seeking is to have much; to have seeking is indeed evil. Even those who seek because they draw near to the Triple Gem do so without knowing [the truth].
One who directly ceases all seeking is a student of the Triple Gem and a Bodhisattva; such a person is able to recognize this.

Sickness. At the outset, do not err yourself and cause others to err. What is meant by "causing others to err"? It refers to those who, lacking understanding, act as teachers regarding the nature of Buddha-nature.
This Buddha-nature is precisely the pure intrinsic nature of sentient beings; because it is not [limited to] sentient beings, it is called Buddha-nature.
Because these are all not the Buddha, it is called the nature of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). The twelve divisions of the scriptures are subsumed within a single phrase or a single verse;
the Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers are opened within the space of a single hair-tip. This is the causal condition for the Bodhisattva precepts.
If one does not realize this, even if one can recite the twelve divisions of the scriptures, one will truly fail to understand them one by one. One.
Regarding the fact that all dharmas are not known: the one is precisely each and every one; all dharmas are precisely one dharma.

If one does not doubt all dharmas, then one can refrain from doubting the nature of sentient beings. If one does not doubt the nature of sentient beings, then one can refrain from doubting the Buddha-nature.

If one does not doubt that which is neither the Buddha-nature nor the nature of sentient beings, then one can refrain from doubting the nature of the Buddha-nature itself. This principle is not within the scope of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding what is understood: the followers of the Two Vehicles know one dharma, yet they do not know all dharmas.
Nevertheless, even though they do not know all dharmas, it cannot be said that they do not know one dharma.
The "double-tongued" holds an incense burner and practices the way of the middle path. He encounters conflict at both ends: attachment to existence and attachment to non-existence.

Those attached to existence take non-attachment to existence as their attachment to non-existence; those attached to non-existence take non-attachment to non-existence as their attachment to existence. Thus they bring about the faults of others.
Thus, to slander others while claiming one's own views are correct is to deceive those who are truly worthy sages; how could such people be subjected to slander or deception?
This person of double-tongued speech does nothing that is not evil.

Not practicing liberation is the fundamental substance of one's prior existence; this is the meaning of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Buddha-nature is the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); the four great elements are the six destinies (*ṣadgati*); the six destinies are one’s parents;
and one’s parents are the eternally abiding Dharma-self (*dharmātman*). In every birth, there is nothing that does not arise from receiving life through them. This is the assembly.
Birth is a phenomenon characterized by impermanence and change. Who is it that gives birth? Who undergoes birth? Who experiences impermanence and change?
It is impossible for there to be a permanent and unchanging dharma. Where there is one who undergoes birth, there is likewise one who undergoes aging, illness, and death.
To perceive a permanent dharma within the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death is to see all the Buddhas.
To seek birth after birth as the eternally abiding Dharma, and to separately seek nirvana, is to kill one’s own parents—that is, to kill one’s own original body.
To practice the karma of releasing living beings is, first, to save those who mistakenly believe there is no birth; this is called preaching the Bodhisattva Precepts.
To seek a lifespan after death that does not perish is to fail to see the Buddha and to create the cause for falling into ruin. Preaching the Bodhisattva Precepts is, first, [to address this].
To rescue those who falsely practice the quest for immortality is called performing the karma of releasing living beings.
Amidst the fires of kalpa that burn the ocean floor and the winds that drive mountains to collide, there remains the true, eternal, and quiescent state—the mark of the bliss of nirvana. Thus it is.
The Bodhisattva, with the eye of the True Dharma, observes that all sentient beings within the vessel-world possess a single, uniform Buddha-nature, which is neither mixed nor subject to decay.
He pays them reverence and circumambulates them, scattering various fragrant flowers upon that place;

this is the mark of the Great Nirvana, not the meaning of death, yet it possesses the meaning of "great death. In it, releasing life is no release, and killing life is no killing; the principle of both is identical.
"Extinguishing" means that if there were one who releases [a victim], then [the victim] was originally not born; if there were one who kills, then [the victim] was originally not dead.
Since parents and sovereigns do not truly die, yet one says they have actually died, this constitutes unfiliality. If it were so, then when another kills, [the victim] is immediately reborn;

when I kill, [the victim] would likewise be reborn. What obstacle would there be to killing? He said: "If when another kills [the victim] is immediately reborn, then retribution is unnecessary; if when I kill [the victim] is likewise reborn, then how could..."
"Kill them! It is like waking from a dream; there is no continuity to the dream-state. If that were so, then he who is born would die immediately;

if I release him, he would also die. What hindrance is there in killing? He replied: "If he who is born dies immediately, then the killer sees him as alive. If I release him, he would also die; yet the one who releases him sees him as being killed.
It is like a nightmare, where there is a method for calling out to end the dream. This Bodhisattva acts within the Illusion-like Samādhi."
They act like illusions, yet they do not grasp at them.
Even those who commit the seven heinous crimes and fall directly into hell—such icchantikas are the great banner of tranquil extinction.
Some say that icchantikas sever their Buddha-nature; yet if an icchantika is itself the Buddha-nature, how could they sever it? This refers to killing an icchantika.

[The opponent] says: "There is no sin [in killing an icchantika]. But how could the Buddha himself kill an icchantika? An external commentary states: "In heaven there are not two suns; among the people there are not two kings;
in a household there are not two masters; in honor there is no second superior. One who commits the seven heinous crimes likely grasps this principle.
If one wishes to commit the seven heinous crimes in all places, one must begin by not keeping slaves or servants oneself;
being arrogant and refusing to request the Dharma from those of low lineage,
the young, those of humble birth, the poor, the lowly, or those with impaired faculties— this is precisely the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
He contemplates his own lineage and gives rise to arrogance; it is simply that he has only recently left the household life and has not yet attained any realization.
This is not something to be censured by the laity, for was he not once a human being in the world?
When interpreting Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas through biased interpretations, one must not dare to give rise to a contemptuous mind, a malicious mind, or a conceited mind toward any sentient being,
let alone toward a novice bodhisattva. As for such novices, they may have already received the precepts before an image of a Buddha or a bodhisattva.

The Buddha. "Shall become a Buddha. This refers to being of one mind with him, manifesting that [enlightenment] is not obtained from another person. If there were no good mind, who would have a good appearance?
A newly initiated bodhisattva may receive the precepts before a Dharma Master; whether the Master can be seen or cannot be seen [is immaterial].
This same single characteristic reveals that [the answer] was not obtained from the Buddha; that is, there is no auspicious sign (*lakṣaṇa*).
Originally, there was only a good intention (*kuśalacitta*). This Dharma Master relies internally upon himself and externally upon others.
When the questioner’s good intention and the auspicious sign appear together, the respondent’s auspicious sign and good intention both become concealed.

To fail to practice and study the Buddha’s relinquishing of false views, his true nature, and his true Dharma-body, while instead engaging in miscellaneous studies, is like discarding gold to pick up rubble.
If one attains right view, the state of correctness, and the true Dharma-body, it does not hinder one from picking up bricks and pebbles and making them into gold; yet,
this is not an exhortation for people to engage in miscellaneous studies, nor is it a matter of lacking skill in knowing the assembly.
Regarding the property of the Triple Gem: it is that which sustains the Buddha’s life of wisdom for both Bodhisattvas and sentient beings;
it is the very property of oneself. Bodhisattvas possess this self, and sentient beings likewise possess this self. Only by recognizing this self can one properly guard it.
To guard it well means nothing other than not using it without measure. The Great Perfect Mirror does not cling to its own nature, nor does it act of its own accord.
The Master initiated the practice of the distinct wisdom and conduct of Samantabhadra and employed it. He applied it to himself and used his own possessions as an example for his eldest son;
this flourished as the family tradition. This is why the Buddha did not enter final nirvana.
A Bodhisattva regards the possessions of others as his own, cherishing them all; whereas ordinary people regard their own possessions as those of others, [neglecting them].
All things are thus violently squandered; when self and other are divided, disputes and litigation arise.
Therefore, by taking all sentient beings as oneself, one causes all sentient beings to recognize themselves; only then can one truly know the multitude.

When receiving offerings and sustenance alone, those who have resided there first are the hosts, while those who arrive later are guests. While the guest has not yet established themselves, they may instead act as host; in such a case, one should provide what is required so that they understand the rules of residence.

Once the guest is able to establish themselves, they may instead act as host to the original resident; in such a case, one should distribute invitations equally so that they understand the absence of fixed residence.

Regarding the Dharma: because there is no duality of essence between guest and host, the long-term resident and the newly arrived, or the dwelling and the non-dwelling, if one does not provide what is required, the guest cannot remain;

this is the fault of the heterodox (tīrthika). If one provides only unevenly for those invited such that the guest can merely stay, this is the fault of the followers of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

As soon as one begins to relish receiving special invitations, one will continue to accept them, gradually becoming secretive and grave. Thus, one turns back the property of the Sangha of the ten directions;

among the eight fields of merit, such property has entered into one’s own possession. Public property should not be used for private purposes—this is what was done upon the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal. —Hé.
It was laid bare like a platter held in one's hands.
He separately invited monks, separately invited five hundred arhats, and the assembly of bodhisattvas; yet these were not as good as the ordinary monk who followed next, for he was not a sage.

All things are difficult to fathom. If one maintains that "this is it," one is still merely making a separate invitation. However, if you recognize the Dharma of the mind-ground, you will recognize the assembly of ordinary beings;
and if you recognize the assembly of ordinary beings, you will recognize the Dharma of the mind-ground. Only then will you know the five hundred arhats and the assembly of bodhisattvas.
This is truly not equal to the Sangha; it is merely the Sangha of ordinary persons. The host sent a foolish boy and mistakenly invited guests;

this is the meaning of "separate invitation. It is called the "Dharma of external paths" because one seeks elsewhere outside the mind; it is said to be "not in accord with the way of filial piety" because one turns one's back on the single source.
The Bodhisattva who lives by wrong livelihood does not even accept food through right livelihood, let alone through wrong livelihood.

Whatever is accomplished through the involvement of mental intention, verbal habituation, and physical action is entirely a phenomenon produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions. To regard these causes and conditions as real phenomena [is the correct view].

To give rise to a mind that grasps at sensation is to combine a hundred kinds of poisonous drugs, a thousand kinds of poisonous drugs, snake venom, the poison of gold and silver, and the poison of sorcery.
By means of these, one seeks to sustain oneself, yet thereby brings about one's own destruction.

If one does not respect the auspicious time and regards the entire body as the Three Jewels, there will be no slanderer because there is no one who is not a relative. When the characteristic of being a relative exists, the self and the Three Jewels become two;
when they become two, this constitutes slander. One then fails to perceive the Three Jewels in all places, for the entire body is suspended in space.
The entirety of emptiness exists within existence. Those who speak of emptiness and those who practice existence thus form two sides;
they do not see emptiness in all places. The entirety of the body exists within auspicious times. There are the three months of fasting and the six days of fasting;
thus there are auspicious times and non-auspicious times, which likewise form two sides; they do not see auspicious times in all places. To analyze this one point:
To destroy the Three Jewels in every place is called taking life. To ruin emptiness in every place is called stealing.

To obstruct and separate from the auspicious moments in every place is called breaking the fast and violating the precepts. What the world calls "revering the auspicious moment" is what the Bodhisattva calls "not revering the auspicious moment.
This is because for the Bodhisattva, there is not even a single kṣaṇa that is not an auspicious moment; thus, they immediately attain everything.
Abiding in emptiness, one perceives the Three Jewels in all places.

When form apprehends the six sense objects, it immediately encompasses the twelve bases and eighteen elements. When form apprehends the five aggregates, it immediately encompasses the seven great elements.
Ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are all deluded regarding form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*).

Failing to see that all places are empty, the Three Jewels are hidden in every place, and the auspicious moments in every place are thereby missed. The sutras frequently cite the two characteristics of male and female to encompass form-dharmas;
this, in turn, encompasses all dharmas, for these are the primary governors of bondage and attachment. This is the gateway for entering the path of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).

To fail to practice the excellent self-nature purity of redemption and, without cause, cast oneself into the six realms of existence is to sell the images of the Buddha, the Bodhisattvas, and one's parents;
it is to sell the Dharma Jewel, the Sangha Jewel, and those who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta— stringing them all together on a single thread and casting them away.

They become officials, or they become slaves. Alas! Within this [world], there are those who sell themselves, those who are plundered and sold by others, those who are able to redeem themselves, and those who await redemption by others.

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas daily go to the borders of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), as well as to all evil persons and bandits, to carry out the work of redeeming people. These non-Buddhists, evil persons, and bandits, or...
If [afflictions] arise within oneself or encounter external conditions, one will certainly be sold and unable to attain liberation.
The ten grave and forty-eight light precepts prevent these from arising internally or encountering external conditions; this is still the second attachment.
If one realizes the purity of self-nature, one may take all non-Buddhists, evil people, and bandits and string them together on a single thread to serve as my officials.
"Make me your slave.
To harm sentient beings is the whole;
the whole of sentient beings is the essence. Suddenly a mass of doubt arises; having already snapped a blade of grass, it becomes a sword.
Carrying staff, bow, and arrows, regarding those of immeasurable greatness, you spontaneously give rise to narrow views. You leap into a light scale and a small bushel;
instead of emptying out the excrement, you pour more in. Relying on your own cleverness, you seize the wealth and property of others.
With every thought you imagine yourself uniquely liberated, yet you are instead bound. When the Buddhas appear before you, you imagine you have achieved success, but it has long since been so.

They cause destruction, merely seeking to counteract cats, wildcats, pigs, and dogs, until the house is filled with chaos; this is truly because they do not recognize that sentient beings nurture such evil habits in this way.

Although the mental application (*vitarka*) and sustained examination (*vicāra*) of unwholesome karma are but minor paths, one must necessarily enter them by means of *vitarka* and *vicāra*. *Vitarka* (mental application) is the alertness that precedes observation;

*vicāra* (sustained examination) is the profound refinement that follows awareness. When entering right *vitarka* and *vicāra*, neither person nor phenomena can be apprehended, even while seeing forms or hearing sounds.
It cannot be apprehended. Skill or clumsiness, victory or defeat, cannot be apprehended. Misfortune or fortune, reliance or concealment, pursuit or avoidance, cannot be apprehended.

The playful exercise of supernatural powers cannot be apprehended. Even profound stillness and immobility cannot be apprehended. To give rise to even a single thought is immediately to employ *vitarka* and *vicāra* as the messengers of thieves.
*Vitarka* and *vicāra* serve as the messengers for all phenomena; yet, *vitarka* and *vicāra* themselves are without fault.

The transgression lies in its misapplication. The Bodhisattva employs *vitarka* and *vicāra* to restrain unwholesome karma; thus, *vitarka* and *vicāra* accomplish the merit of fulfilling one's mission.
To momentarily conceive of the Lesser Vehicle [is the error].
A person of good faith in the Mahāyāna simply believes that I am the Buddha. That I am the Buddha does not mean that sentient beings are not Buddhas;
rather, the Buddha, I, and all sentient beings are one and the same in this single mind. Thought arises from the mind, and the mind returns to thought;
for thought after thought never leaves the mind, it is like every drop returning to its source. Those of the Two Vehicles do not dare to employ this continuous mind.

The Bodhisattva is able to employ the continuous mind because he penetrates and perceives the source of all phenomena. Thus, according to the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), rivers are the source and the ocean is the outflow;
according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the ocean is the source and the rivers are the outflow. The entire dharma-realm is this mind.
How could there be a thought of exiting the dharma-realm? Even if a hair’s breadth of doubt were momentarily to arise, it would result entirely in the manifestation of differentiated marks;
for one perceives going where there is no place to go, and employs continuity where there is no continuity.
Not giving rise to the deluded thoughts of sentient beings is itself the great vow of a bodhisattva.

All the *pāramitās* are held in a single hand by the bodhisattva, never forsaking them for even a single thought-moment. This is because they employ poverty entirely and employ attachment entirely, yet they have never been different from that one [vow].
The mind is the parents, the teachers, and the monastics; it is solely the Triple Gem. It is not a dharma of the single mind; it is neither teacher nor friend.
It is not a dharma of the single mind; it is neither sutra nor vinaya. It is not a dharma of the single mind; it is neither dwelling nor practice, neither direction nor stage.

It is not a dharma of the single mind; it is neither understanding nor practice, nor the observance of precepts. Thus, this great vow shall continue until the end of the future, never departing from the single mind.
The mind: though its vows are vast, they are difficult to bring to completion; the mind, however, is concise and easy to govern.

This mind is the true mark (*dharmatā*); therefore, it is not called a deluded mind. It is the mark of original existence; therefore, it is not called a greedy mind. It is the mark of firmness and immovability;
therefore, it is not called attachment.

The mind is but a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). A single thought-moment contains the three periods of time; therefore, it is called "thought after thought. Thought after thought does not depart from the mind, for it is fundamentally but a single thought-moment.
The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended.
If there were a past, present, and future, then there would be nothing that could not be apprehended. Since there is no past, present, or future...

It comes; yet there is nothing that cannot be attained. Within every thought-moment, the Bodhisattva has no seeing, no non-seeing, no seeing that can be attained, and no seeing that cannot be attained. This is what is called "one thought-moment."
A vow is not easily made;
once made, it is not easily maintained. This is because of the beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). One must therefore urge oneself with a sense of urgency and resolve to maintain it.

Although the breaking of precepts arises from body and mind, the transgression of the precepts is not itself a fault of body and mind; nor is the maintaining of the precepts [a virtue of body and mind].
The efficacy of body and mind: if one breaks the precepts with this body and mind, then one has broken the precepts;
if one does not break the precepts with this body and mind, then one maintains the precepts. Whether it is by means of this or not by means of this, it pertains to this single person.

Yet this single person is neither capable of merit nor capable of transgression. Why? Because this single person is both body and mind, and yet not body and mind; both by means of them and not by means of them; and yet both.

It is neither by means of nor not by means of; it is both maintaining and destroying, and neither maintaining nor destroying; it is both the Buddha and sentient beings, and neither the Buddha nor sentient beings;
it is both accomplished and unaccomplished, and neither accomplished nor unaccomplished;
it is both this single person and not this single person. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "This Dharma is beyond the reach of thought, deliberation, or discrimination."

It is precisely that which does not employ conceptualization or discrimination. Although it does not employ conceptualization or discrimination, it is not something that can be reached by conceptualization or discrimination.
Furthermore, how could that which employs conceptualization and discrimination be something reachable by conceptualization and discrimination?

Setting aside for a moment whether one employs or does not employ them, the very act of present conceptualization and discrimination is itself non-conceptualization and non-discrimination. Moreover, how could it be...
Can that which is reached by means of practice or non-practice be fathomed?
Previously it was said, "To make all vows, vowing to be filial and obedient toward parents, teachers, and monks"; here it is said, "Vowing for all sentient beings."
All shall attain Buddhahood. From head to tail, it is the same. Those who give birth to me are my parents; those who bring me to fulfillment are my teachers and monks.
Taking self-nature purity as the essence of the precepts, since all sentient beings possess the significance of being one's parents and teachers, one gives rise to this impartial and universal vow;
this is called filial piety that pervades all places. Chen Ping said: "It was not because of Wei Wuzhi."
"How have you been able to advance so far? Emperor Gao said, "If you are such as this, you may truly be called one who does not turn his back on his roots.

You have traveled through hardships with your own nature pure and clear, never for a single moment being separated from the four modes of deportment. To abandon one's own nature is to enter into evil."
Within the boundaries of the kingdom, one perceives an evil king; this is what is entangled by the net of doubt. Because the self-nature of doubt is equal, one perceives high and low.
Because the self-nature of doubt is manifest, one perceives depth. Because the self-nature of doubt is great compassion, one perceives lions, tigers, and wolves.
Because the self-nature of doubt is great meditative concentration, one perceives the calamities of water, fire, and wind. Because the self-nature of doubt is non-existent, one [perceives...]
Seeing a bandit, one does not doubt the unimpeded nature of reality; thus, seeing a venomous snake, one does not harbor even a single moment’s doubt regarding the purity of intrinsic nature.
Consequently, there is not so much as an inch of ground that is a difficult place for travel. There is liberation in this very place; there is quiescence in this very place.

With every lifting and lowering of the foot, there is nothing that is not a state of settled dwelling (*āraṇyaka*). To practice the summer retreat (*vassa*) is seen as practicing travel; to see [the world] as traveling is seen as practicing oneness.
In all difficult circumstances, one sees that all difficulties arise from the bonds of views; it is simply that precepts give rise to divergent opinions.

To deviate from the proper order of honor and humility—wherein all phenomena have old and young, noble and base—is to prioritize them based on such distinctions. In my Dharma, there is no [such thing].
Each possesses the three periods of time. Who among them is young? Each possesses the three periods of time. Who among them is old? Each possesses one Buddha-nature.
Who among them is lowly? Each possesses one Buddha-nature. Who among them is noble? It is only by the sequence of receiving the precepts that there is priority or posteriority;
thus, the one Vairocana and the billions of Śākyamunis, as well as immeasurable sentient beings, enter into Bodhi.
Within the path of the Bodhisattva, like a vermilion pearl banner, successive reflections appear; all are observed with a single flavor and equality.
Where there is no before or after, one manifests before and after, establishing an order through the distinction of honor and humility, and likewise forming honor and humility because of that order.
When the Buddha was walking and circumambulating a stūpa, Ānanda asked, "Whose stūpa is this? The Buddha replied, "It is the stūpa of a past Buddha. Ānanda...
[Ananda] asked, "Whose disciple is he? The Buddha said, "He is my disciple. Ananda said, "It must be so.

He does not cultivate the foundation of merit and wisdom that establishes consciousness; rather, his ocean of wisdom reflects intermingled lights. He expounds upon the foundation of consciousness, and his field of merit is fully laden. How is this possible?"
This is the fundamental text. It inquires about all places where beings practice the Path; it inquires about all sentient beings and the states of suffering, calamity, death, and extinction;

it inquires about all great fires and great waters, black winds and rākṣasas, and all people who receive retribution for their sins—those with excessive lust, excessive anger, excessive ignorance, and those with many illnesses.

The *Jianze shoujie shu* (Commentary on the Selection for Receiving Precepts) states: "If one’s physical form is not as it should be, one must select [and exclude] accordingly; if one’s karmic obstructions are not as they should be, one must select [and exclude] accordingly.
This is merely selecting that which is selectable and choosing that which is choosable. As for the seed of Buddha-nature, there is simply no place to apply the hand."
The renunciant who understands this meaning does not bow to kings, nor to parents;

he does not show respect to his six kin, nor offer salutations to ghosts and spirits, yet this is not considered an overstepping of bounds. That Bodhisattva Dharma Master intended to take action upon the ordination platform;
as soon as the thought arose, he lost both his eyes.
Once you recognize what it means to be "dyed with a ruined color," you will understand the Master’s words. What is meant by being "dyed with a ruined color"? All dyeing is it.
When the people of the country conceal their dyeing, they reveal all that is true; when the bhikṣus conceal the truth, they reveal all that is ruined.
The Bodhisattva perceives ruin within the unruined and perceives the unruined within the ruined, yet remains unstained by either—this is the Master’s words. (Yunqi Bianzhi)
Regarding the impropriety of receiving the Bodhisattva precepts: it is not inherently improper to receive the Bodhisattva precepts directly upon understanding the Dharma Master’s words;
nor is it inherently improper not to receive the Bodhisattva precepts even while understanding the Dharma Master’s words.
It is simply that such individuals are rarely encountered.
To benefit others, he acted as a teacher;

though this great mirror could not recognize a single character, he attained the meaning within the Dharma. If one were to lecture based on the text or proclaim it according to the written records, this would merely be a pretense of being able to understand.
Within the Dharma there is no separate "meaning"; the meaning resides within the Dharma. That which is the meaning within the Dharma is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
There is the conventional truth, yet the ultimate truth is non-existent. Within the ultimate, the acquired nature is non-existent, yet existence has the acquired nature;

the innate nature is non-existent, yet existence has the innate nature; the innate nature is non-existent, yet existence has the innate nature; the path-nature is non-existent, yet existence has the path-nature; the True Dharma is non-existent, yet existence has the True Dharma;
thus, the aspiration for enlightenment is non-existent, yet existence has the aspiration for enlightenment; and nurturing is non-existent, yet existence has nurturing.
The nature that cannot be destroyed is indestructible. Within it, the practice of contemplation has no entering or exiting; yet within the practice of contemplation, there is entering and exiting.
There are ten factors of dhyāna, neither more nor less. There is not a single factor of dhyāna that possesses ten, nor even hundreds or thousands.

When the mind is active, the dharmas are naturally active; when the dharmas cease, the mind also ceases. One who attains the mind within the dharmas may, through the seven obscurations, [attain liberation].
Receiving the precepts in this present life, a bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense can establish himself in the realization of non-arising.

There are no precepts to be maintained, no offenses to be extinguished, and no auspicious signs to be seen. There are no thirty minds or ten stages to be traversed, and no wondrous enlightenment to be attained.
To explain the Buddha-nature to evildoers is like the principle of having a king. Within the minds of sentient beings there is Buddha-nature;
it cannot be that the people of a country have no king within their hearts. Suppose a man traveling on a road were asked, "Do you have a king? and he replied, "I have no king."
Then there would inevitably be a punishment for unrighteousness. Within the hearts of ordinary people, all possess the King [the Buddha-nature]. Such is the meaning of the Buddha-nature.
If one were to seize an ordinary person and, from head to toe, divide them into threads and cut them into fibers to seek the form of the King, it would seem utterly impossible to find.
The principle that sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature is likewise. Yet, those of external paths and heterodox views consequently claim that sentient beings...
In the mind of one who has taken birth, there is no Buddha-nature. He said to the king:
"If all the people within your kingdom were to possess your royal authority, you would be joyful;

if all the people within your kingdom were to lack your royal authority, you would be angry. Yet when you speak to those many people within your kingdom, they merely listen with indifference and remain unconcerned."

This is irrelevant. If one were to commit an offense against the sovereign by inciting rebellion, those among the people of that many lands who have the king in their hearts would be angered, while those among the people of that many lands who do not have the king in their hearts would rejoice.

When a bodhisattva acts as a king, he preaches the precepts of the Buddha-nature; however, he does not preach them to those who have not received the bodhisattva precepts, nor to non-Buddhists or evil persons.
The same applies to the explanation of their meaning.

There is not a single person, nor a single moment, in which one who receives these Buddha-precepts while walking upon the ground of a king without a sense of shame does not tread upon emptiness at every step.
Should they give rise to a thought of violating the precepts, footprints immediately appear; when they come, ghosts block their way, and when they go, ghosts [obstruct them].
"Having swept it, you drank the king’s water, which was transformed into a fierce fire; thus, the offerings of the donor have entirely become the dregs of the three evil realms.
Yet the king’s land and the king’s water remain exactly as they were, down to every single speck of dust and drop of liquid. From where did these traces in the air come?
Space is fundamentally traceless and cannot be swept. To recognize this distinction between the inverted and the non-inverted is [the truth]."
The thieves are ghosts; they all stand before the majestic lion throne of the Celestial Light.

They do not offer the scriptures, nor skin, blood, marrow, or bone. That which is difficult to relinquish, they are able to relinquish. It is not necessary to perceive them as pen, ink, or paper; there are immediately both the characters and their meaning.
This applies to the entire scripture. When bamboo, wood, silk, or paper have not yet been used for writing, one does not say, "Write the precepts for me.

Once they have been written upon, one does not say, "I have written the precepts. When the seven-jeweled casket or bag has not yet been used to contain them, one does not say, "Place the scripture in it for me.
Once it has been placed therein, one does not say, "I have placed the scripture in it. This is the complete embodiment of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

If a bodhisattva perceives the upholding [of precepts] as "upholding," this is called being single-minded; however, if they perceive making offerings as "making offerings," it is not in accordance with the Dharma,
nor does it transform sentient beings.
"You are an animal; arouse the bodhicitta. If an animal lacks the bodhicitta, there is nothing that can be aroused.
If it possesses the bodhicitta, how could it be aroused? Have you not heard the Bodhisattva address someone as "You are an animal"?
Why did he not simply say, "You are not an animal"? If one is not an animal, what is one? And if one is an animal, what else is there?
Do not trouble yourself with excessive complications.
When expounding the Dharma, do not rely on the literal letter;
the Dharma has both prohibitions and affirmations. Regard the audience as the manifestation of sentient beings, while your own true body is Vairocana, never for a single moment otherwise.
He does not manifest in a grand or ostentatious manner; this is the mark of the invisible crown (*anavalokitamūrdha*). Because sentient beings do not see it, he speaks of it to represent it.

The Dharma Master manifests the form of Vairocana, while the audience manifests the forms of the thousand-billion Śākyamunis. The dharma-nature and essence of the body of a single sentient being are thus;
the dharma-nature and essence of the body of each and every sentient being are thus. By uniting the bodies of each and every sentient being, [one becomes...]
The dharma-characteristic of the single body is such by its very nature. If one were to abandon the high seat and so forth and stand upon level ground, there would be nothing to manifest.
The thousand Śākyamunis emerge from the Lotus-Womb World and enter the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature Emptiness;
therein, neither Vairocana nor Śākyamuni is seen. This is the meaning of "concealment. They then emerge from the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature Emptiness.
Samādhi. Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, one perceives Vairocana within Śākyamuni; among the assembly of listeners, one perceives the thousand Śākyamunis. This is the manifestation of meaning.
That which should be negated is manifested, and that which should be manifested is negated; this is called "speaking at the improper time.
Is there anyone capable of being a listener to that which is neither spoken nor shown? When both negation and manifestation are set aside, it accords with the Dharma at all times.
The world of dharmas is empty by way of non-dharma-restriction; the land is empty; sentient beings are empty. These three jewels are the dharma of emptiness, boundless and immeasurable.

Within this emptiness, one might take a single vessel of emptiness and say, "This is a portion of that emptiness," yet one cannot increase it by even a single fraction. In each and every [instance],...
The flask. Establishing the number of flasks. Establishing the number of emptinesses within the flasks. To say, "This is the emptiness of that portion;

one cannot increase it by even a single part," is the foolish dharma of the white-robed laypeople. The Śrāvakas have a dharma of restrictive limits. This is the number of the Triple Gem; this is not the number of the Triple Gem.
This attains the Triple Gem; this loses the Triple Gem. This possesses the Triple Gem; this lacks the Triple Gem. This is called "not."

The Dharma is limited by its own nature. For a Bodhisattva, there is no limitation in receiving, no limitation in giving, no limitation in gathering and taking in, no limitation in training, no limitation in teaching, no limitation in direction, and no limitation in time.

Because the Dharma cannot be limited, the Three Jewels are immeasurable. A small portion is set aside as the Three Jewels; they are as boundless as space. A small portion is analyzed and established as...
Emptiness cannot be analyzed away; the Triple Gem cannot be cut asunder; the Dharma cannot be destroyed. It is only because of the views of "is" and "is not" that one is defiled by them.

Therefore it is said: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; it manifests dharmas equal to empty space; when the realization of empty space is attained, there is neither 'is' nor 'is not. Alas!
Were it not for those of keen faculties and superior wisdom, how could one possibly realize this?
It shatters the self-nature of dharmas; it is primordially liberated. The Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas are established to restrain what is improper.
That which is primordially pure is simply its original liberation. Therefore, one employs the precepts through the nature, rather than employing the nature through the precepts.
The Bodhisattva employs all dharmas without attachment. He gives rise to the bodhicitta without attachment to the bodhicitta;
he practices the six pāramitās without attachment to the six pāramitās; and he attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
One does not cling to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. When preaching the Dharma, one does not cling to the preaching of the Dharma;

when delivering sentient beings, one does not cling to the delivering of sentient beings. Where there is clinging, there is breaking; where there is grasping, there is attachment. This is the conclusion of the precepts in this sutra: as they are established, they are swept away.
From beginning to end, one uses the nature through the precepts, rather than using the precepts to define the nature. This is because the mind is the master. Whenever the precepts are established...
Regarding the Śrāvaka precepts, the faults of the turbid storehouse are explained; regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, the faults of the pure extreme are explained.
The Śrāvaka precepts are taught for ordinary persons, whereas the Bodhisattva precepts are not taught even for sages. Thus, they cannot be treated as identical examples.
Regarding the dissemination section of this sutra,
the nature of water as a substance begins as a mere trickle, develops into rivers and streams, and ultimately returns to the vast ocean; thus, it possesses the capacity for flow.

Only after there is the power to penetrate can there be penetration; yet even when something becomes obstructed, blocked, and ceases to flow, there must likewise be the power to penetrate before it can flow again.
Therefore, first, "flowing" implies "penetration," and second, "penetration" implies "flowing.

That flowing implies penetration is the meaning of *xing* (nature); that penetration implies flowing is the meaning of *jiao* (teaching); and that flowing implies penetration is the meaning of *benjue* (original enlightenment).
That which flows through penetration is the meaning of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya*). The meaning of precepts first penetrates and subsequently flows;
yet, for this flow to continue, there can be no flow without penetration. Therefore, the One Honored One is established within the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
This Buddha-nature, the ever-abiding scroll of precepts, has always resided within the minds of all sentient beings. One must shatter these fine motes of dust and bring it forth.

In the Great Sūtra, the Buddha permits his own penetration, and sentient beings begin to receive its flow. Once sentient beings have received its flow, they likewise each permit their own penetration.
Thus, transformation follows transformation without end; this is the natural law (*dharmatā*) of sentient beings, and it is the natural law of the Buddhas of the thousand worlds.
Vairocana manifests as Śākyamuni, and Śākyamuni manifests as Vairocana. This is through immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*).

They emerge from the ordinary abodes of sentient beings and constantly practice therein. As it is for one sentient being, so it is for a thousand, a hundred billion, and even for as many sentient beings as there are atoms.
As it is for one Buddha, so it is for a thousand, a hundred billion, and even for as many Buddhas as there are atoms.
As it is for one world, so it is for a thousand, a hundred billion, and even for as many worlds as there are atoms.
It is so. One treasury of the Dharma is thus; a thousand, ten thousand, or a billion treasuries of the Dharma are thus; even a dust mote’s worth of treasuries of the Dharma is likewise.

This refers to the gates of the Dharma that are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and are ineffable. To briefly open them by the measure of a single hair-tip is yet for that hair-tip not to be established at all.
This is the ultimate penetration. While the hair-tip is not established, the sands of the Ganges are not [diminished].
The Dharma-gate may be taught; all things are established together herein. This is the ultimate point of this flow. Without the capacity to penetrate, there would be nothing to flow;
without the capacity to flow, there would be nothing to penetrate. All Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas receive [this teaching] from all sentient beings.
Thus ends the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as described above.
The "Tathāgatagarbha of the Constant Abiding of Cause-and-Effect Buddha-nature.
The commentary divides this into two parts. However, cause-and-effect is itself the Buddha-nature’s constant abiding; there is nothing that can be divided.
Cause-and-effect is itself the liberation-Buddha-nature, the constant abiding of Prajñā, and the constant abiding of Nirvāṇa. It is...
Prajñā-buddha-nature is the cause and fruit of liberation; it is the cause and fruit of quiescent extinction. It is Prajñā-buddha-nature;
it is quiescent extinction and eternal abiding. It is liberation—neither three nor not-three, neither one nor not-one. All the treasuries of dharmas are explained in this very way.
